A later analysis of the Eskridge-Baer data found that one puzzle might have a 
simple answer: the Supreme Court discussed Chevron when that issue was 
raised by the parties or amici. See Natalie Salmanowitz & Holger Spamann 
Does the Supreme Court Really Not Apply Chevron When it Should'^, 57 INT’L 
Re v . L. & ECON. 81 (2019).
At the court-of-appeals level, Professors Barnett and Walker found fidelity 
to the Chevron deference regime after a study of circuit court opinions over the 
decade 2003—2013. See Kent Barnett & Christopher Walker, Chevron in the 
Circuit Courts, 116 MiCH. L. Re v . 1 (2017). Some, but not all, other studies of 
court-of-appeals decisions found that the choice of deference regime affected 
outcomes. See Orin S. Kerr, Shedding Light on Chevron: An Empirical Study 
of the Chevron Doctrine in the U.S. Courts of Appeals, 15 Ya l e J. On  Re g . 1 
(1998) (examining court-of-appeals decisions for the years 1995 and 1996); 
Peter H. Schuck & E. Donald Elliott, To the Chevron Station: An Empirical 
Study of Federal Administrative Law, 1990 DUKE L. J. 984 (finding, based on 
a study of all decisions, not just those citing Chevron, that during the six 
months foUcvvring Chevron, courts of appeals upheld agency decisions 10 
percent more often than in the previous six months); Thomas J. Miles & Cass 
R. Sunstein, Do Judges Make Regulatory Policy? An Empirical Investigation of 
Chevron, 73 U. Ch i. L. Re v . 823 (2006). For a qualitative assessment of 
Chevron's slow rise to prominence in the federal courts of appeals, see Gary 
Lawson & Stephen Kam, Making Law out of Nothing at All: The Origins of the 
Chevron Doctrine, 65 Ad min . L. Re v . 1, 33—50 (2013).
6. 
The Law-Fact Distinction. Loper Bright asserts that, under pre-APA 
precedents “the Court often treated agency determinations of fact as binding 
on the courts,” even while it resolved questions of law using independent 
judgment. The opinion thus calls for courts to police the line between law and 
fact in a manner that was, perhaps, not quite as necessary in the Chevron era. 
That is because, to the extent that the Court adopted a deferential standard 
for (many) questions of law before Loper Bright, it was unnecessary to draw a 
precise line between questions of law and questions of fact. After all, regardless 
of the side on which a particular question was categorized, the standard of 
review was deferential. Loper Bright, however, appears to distinguish between 
deferential review of questions of fact and de novo review of questions of law. 
To be sure, Loper Bright acknowledged that cases hke Gray v. Powell and 
Hearst “applied deferential review upon concluding that a particular statute 
empowered an agency to decide how a broad statutory term applied to specific 
facts found by the agency.” But Chief Justice Roberts claimed that those cases 
involved deferential review “cabined to factbound determinations.”
As a result, Loper Bright might put added pressure on the importance of 
distinguishing between the categories of fact and law. Or it might raise the 
question of how to categorize “mixed questions of law and fact,” to the extent 
those remain a separate category under Loper Bright's framework.
